sections.title: Socialism and the City from the Gilded Age to Mayor Mamdani
sections.description: How have socialists and labor radicals in the United States challenged and taken power at the local level? This course considers the relationship between economic processes, radical political visions, and concrete organizing strategies, from the late nineteenth century to the present. Socialist and labor radical movements in this period sought at times to remake local communities and at others to shape national developments, often looking abroad for inspiration and models of municipal politics. Starting with early "municipal socialism" along the Great Lakes and among the mining towns of Montana, the course then considers the revival of socialist politics at the local level in the 1930s-40s, and post-WWII continuities of left localism in places like Milwaukee, WI, Richmond, CA, Jackson, MS, and, most recently, the democratic socialist project in New York City. Along the way, it examines the opportunities and challenges that local politics and power have presented to socialists whose visions largely extended beyond city lines even as their administrative tools rarely did.
